title: Quantile-Anchored Headroom Orchestrator for Dedicated Fleets
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Dedicated customers require predictable throughput and SLOs, but current autoscalers either over-provision (cost blowouts) or oscillate under bursty token workloads. We need a policy engine that: 1) expresses targets as service-level percentiles (p50/p90/p99 token latency and throughput), 2) compiles those targets into per-fleet headroom reservations, and 3) enforces safety limits to prevent destructive scaling (rapid flapping, runaway capacity growth).

Proposal: Build the Quantile-Anchored Headroom Orchestrator (AQH). AQH combines quantile-based demand estimation with a bounded allocation and emergency venting layer. Key concepts: 
- Anchored quantiles: maintain rolling-window percentiles for token latency and tokens/sec (multi-window: 1m, 5m, 30m) and anchor allocations to a conservative percentile (e.g., p90 anchored to p95 warmup).
- Headroom crediting: translate anchored quantiles into headroom tokens (instance-minutes) using model-specific throughput profiles and KV cache locality factors.
- Safety envelope: hard limits on ramp-rate (instances/min), budget cap (max instances per fleet), and progressive backoff windows after rollbacks.
- Venting & graceful degradation: when headroom is exhausted and demand spikes, evict/shape low-priority queues and degrade non-critical features (embeddings batch windows, background reranks) before scaling beyond budget.
- Fallback model variants: use cheaper quantized variants automatically as an intermediate cost-speed lever when scaling is unsafe.

Why different: Unlike simple PID or single-metric autoscalers, AQH fuses percentile-driven demand signals with cost-aware conversion to capacity units and an explicit emergency venting strategy. That permits predictable SLO adherence while bounding cost and avoiding oscillation in noisy token workloads.
acceptance_criteria: AQH prototype compiles p90 token-latency + throughput targets into a headroom plan (instance-minutes) for a sample fleet
Simulator can replay 30 representative traces (including sudden 10x bursts) and show: <5% SLO violations for p90, <10% CPU/RAM overruns, and no more than 2 emergency scale events/hour
Safety envelope enforces a ramp-rate limit and prevents >25% capacity growth in any 5-minute window without manual approval
Integrations: headroom metrics emitted to console dashboards (token headroom, credit balance, venting events) and audit log entries for every enforced scale decision
Documentation: design doc published, console feature flag for private fleets, runbook for operator-driven rollback and incident follow-up
progress_updates: 2026-02-20: Initial design sketch completed; shared with SRE and PM. Received feedback to tighten ramp-rate and to include warmup lanes for KV-affinity.
2026-02-27: Prototype simulator skeleton implemented (Go). First synthetic trace run showed oscillation when using raw p90 without smoothing.
2026-03-03: Introduced multi-window smoothing (1m/5m/30m) and an anchored uplift factor (default +15% headroom). Oscillation reduced in simulator runs.
2026-03-08: Implemented emergency venting prototype: identifies victim queues and emits venting events to metrics. Integration test with dedicated-staging passed basic behavior checks.
2026-03-10: Security reviewed the fallback model variant path; no secrets exposure. Risk: quantized variants require per-tenant performance validation to avoid regressions.
decisions: Use anchored percentiles (p90 -> p95 warmup anchor) rather than raw percentiles to reduce sensitivity to transient spikes
Headroom will be expressed in instance-minutes and converted from tokens/sec using model throughput table maintained in runtime config
Ramp-rate default: 5% of committed fleet per minute with a hard cap of 10 instances/min for small fleets; configurable per-contract
Emergency venting precedes any ad-hoc capacity expansion beyond committed headroom; venting is policy-driven and observable
Fallback variant selection will be risk-scored; only auto-deploy quantized variants when regression risk < low and customer opt-in is true for private deployments
risks_and_mitigation: Oscillation risk: mitigated by multi-window smoothing + anchor uplift + cooldown windows
Cost blowout: mitigated by budget caps and percentage-of-commit guardrails; provide visibility and manual override to finance/ops
Quality regressions from variant fallback: require A/B rollout and per-tenant evals; add rollback hooks to console
KV cache affinity loss on scale-out: mitigate by preferring warmup lanes and KV-affinity scored allocation when possible
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (2 weeks): Simulator improvements and quantitative validation against historical traces. Deliver: simulator reports + acceptance signal
Phase 2 (3 weeks): Policy compiler and headroom converter implemented in control plane; add metric emissions and console visualization
Phase 3 (2 weeks): Safety envelope enforcement and venting actions wired into fleet controller; add audit logs and operator runbook
Phase 4 (2 weeks): Canary rollout to low-risk dedicated customers with monitoring and automatic rollback criteria
Phase 5 (ongoing): Iterate on uplift factors, add ML-based demand forecaster as optional input, and expand to multi-region awareness
qa_plan: Unit tests for headroom conversion math and ramp-rate clamps
Simulator regression suite with recorded customer traffic traces
Chaos tests: random network partitions and delayed metrics to ensure safety envelope holds
Canary with synthetic and real traffic; 24/7 on-call during canary window
comments: Marco Chen (2026-02-28): Simulator run 5 shows noisy latency on model 'redwood-7b' when mem pressure > 75%. Need to factor instance memory headroom into the headroom conversion.
Priya Rao (SRE, 2026-03-01): Agree with ramp-rate defaults; also recommend a minimum cooldown of 90s per policy change to avoid API churn on the fleet controller.
Elena Garcia (PM, 2026-03-05): For Dedicated customers, surface cost impact estimate per proposed headroom change in the console before committing scale operations.
